Indistinguishable flowers either have no visible petal-like parts or the parts are so small that it is difficult to make out their number of arrangement. A flower may be very small and still have parts that are quite discernible.

Irregular flowers are not radially symmetrical; that is, their petals or petal-like parts are not similar in size, shape or color. Usually, these flowers have upper and lower parts that are called lips.
Wildflowers with stem leaves that are arranged singly on the stem, first at one point and then at another, they are alternate. If there is only one stem leaf, it is considered alternate.

Wildflowers with stem leaves growing directly across from each other that are either in pairs or in circles of threes, fours, fives or more are opposite or whorled. If there is only one stem leaf, it is considered alternate.
Leaves growing from the base of the plant are basal leaves.
A vine is a plant with long trailing, twining or climbing stems generally over two feet long.
A shrub is a plant with woody stem permanently above the ground, but at maturity it is usually under ten feet high.
If the margin of a leaf is even and unbroken, the leaf is said to be entire.

If the margin has more or less regular, shallow indentations, the leaf is toothed. The leaves of some plants have one or more deeper indentations, which separate the leaf into several sections known as lobes.

Often a leaf is actually divided into separate parts known as leaflets. If some of the leave indentations go almost to the midrib, even though the divisions are not strictly leaflets, the leaf is considered to be divided.
